titolo: Madoff – How a $65 Billion Fraud Hid for Decades
descrizione:
Bernard Madoff ran the largest Ponzi scheme ever uncovered. When it collapsed in December 2008, investors' account statements showed about $65 billion in paper wealth, most of it never real. This investigation follows how the fraud worked, why regulators missed it for years, and who paid the price.

Using SEC filings, court records and major news reporting, we trace the timeline from Madoff's rise on Wall Street to his arrest on December 11, 2008, his guilty plea in March 2009 and his 150-year sentence, and look at the lessons for investors and regulators.

fatti: Statements at Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities showed about $65 billion in client balances when the firm collapsed in December 2008
The balances were largely fictitious
Open loop: how did this stay hidden for decades, and where did the money go?
Madoff founded his firm in 1960
He became a prominent market-making figure and was non-executive chairman of NASDAQ in the early 1990s
His firm's legitimate market-making business operated alongside the separate investment advisory business
The advisory business was run on the 17th floor of the Lipstick Building in Manhattan
Madoff claimed a 'split-strike conversion' strategy of buying stocks and using options
Returns were reported as unusually smooth, roughly 10–12% a year according to reporting
Many investors came through feeder funds and word of mouth
Auditing was done by Friehling & Horowitz, a tiny firm
Investor money was not invested as claimed
New deposits were used to pay redemptions to earlier investors
Trades shown on statements were fabricated
The scheme required constant inflows to survive
Madoff told his sons on December 10, 2008 that it was 'one big lie' according to the criminal complaint
Harry Markopolos submitted analysis to the SEC in 2000, and again in 2001, 2005 and 2007
The SEC conducted examinations and investigations of Madoff's firm but did not uncover the fraud
The SEC Inspector General's 2009 report found the agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation despite credible red flags
Madoff's firm acted as its own custodian and executed trades itself, so no independent party verified the trades
The 2008 financial crisis triggered heavy redemption requests from investors
Reports indicate redemption requests of about $7 billion in late 2008
Madoff did not have the cash to meet them
On December 10, 2008 he confessed to his sons
Madoff was arrested by the FBI on December 11, 2008
He was charged with securities fraud
He was released on bail under home confinement after his arrest, and was jailed without bail after the court revoked it on March 12, 2009
He pleaded guilty to 11 felony counts on March 12, 2009
Judge Denny Chin sentenced Madoff to 150 years in prison on June 29, 2009
He was ordered to forfeit about $170 billion in assets, a figure that was largely symbolic
He died in federal custody on April 14, 2021
Trustee Irving Picard was appointed to recover funds for victims through the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC)
The $65 billion figure represented fictitious paper balances; actual principal losses were about $17–20 billion according to the trustee
As of recent trustee updates, recoveries exceed $14 billion for victims
Thousands of investors including charities, pension funds and individuals were affected
Consistent, too-smooth returns and secrecy were red flags
Independent custody, reputable auditors and verifiable trades are key safeguards
Regulatory reforms followed, including SEC internal changes
The loop closes: the fraud survived because trust replaced verification

_correzioni: Chapter 'The Man Everyone Trusted': 'non-executive chairman of NASDAQ in the early 1990s' is correct (he chaired it in 1990, 1991 and 1993), so it is kept as is.

Chapter 'Warnings Ignored': Markopolos's submissions were in 2000, 2001, 2005 and 2007 (the 2001 one was via the SEC's Boston office; 2000 was to the SEC's Boston office), which is acceptable and kept as is.

Chapter 'Warnings Ignored': 'Bernard Madoff was never required to prove trades with independent custody' is a vague, partly unsupported claim, so it was rewritten as: 'Madoff's firm acted as its own custodian and executed trades itself, so no independent party verified the trades'.

Chapter 'The Sentence': the forfeiture order was $170.8 billion, so 'about $170 billion' is kept. The claim 'a figure reflecting the scale of the fraud' was rewritten as 'a figure that was largely symbolic'.

Chapter 'Arrest': the claim 'held without bail after the court revoked his home confinement' was corrected: bail was revoked on March 12, 2009 at the plea hearing, not at arrest. After his arrest on Dec 11, 2008 he was released on $10 million bail under home confinement. The sentence now says this.
Chapter 'Where the Money Went': 'actual principal losses were about $17–20 billion' is supported by the trustee (about $17.5 billion in principal lost). Kept as is.

Chapter 'Where the Money Went': 'recoveries exceed $14 billion' is supported (the trustee's total recoveries have been about $14.3 billion as of the early 2020s), so it is kept but the phrasing 'as of recent trustee updates' is retained.
Chapter '2008: The Run': redemption requests of about $7 billion are widely reported (about $7 billion), so it is kept; wording 'Reports indicate' retained.
Chapter 'The Promise of Steady Returns': returns of roughly 10-12% a year, as widely reported, are kept.
Chapter 'Arrest': 'He was charged with securities fraud' is correct (a single count in the complaint). Kept.
Chapter 'How the Scheme Worked': the quote 'one big lie' attributed to Dec 10, 2008, to his sons per the criminal complaint is accurate. Kept.
